claims.text: The Mg–Ti–Zn alloy initially has a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
The initial solid solution is homogeneous and FCC, with minimal intermetallic phases.
Isothermal annealing causes progressive precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds in the Mg–Ti–Zn alloy.
The annealing-induced precipitation is diffusion controlled.
Mg–Ti–Zn alloys can contain intermetallic compounds.
The precipitates are specifically Mg-rich phases such as Mg2Ti or Mg–Zn compounds.
Intermetallic precipitation progressively depletes Mg from the surrounding metastable matrix.
Matrix Mg depletion impairs formation and maintenance of a coherent protective oxide or passive layer.
A continuous oxide film can inhibit further oxidation by limiting oxygen transport.
Loss of the protective oxide or passive layer reduces both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial alloy has robust corrosion and oxidation resistance because retained Mg supports protective passivation.
Shorter or lower-temperature annealing produces only partial intermetallic clustering and leaves enough matrix Mg for effective oxide-film formation.
Longer or higher-temperature annealing produces extensive intermetallic precipitation, substantial Mg depletion, and a marked decline in corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The service-relevant regime for this Mg–Ti–Zn alloy is 300–550 °C for exposures of 1–20 hours.
Both short peak-temperature exposure and extended exposure at lower temperatures can matter when assessing microstructural stability in elevated-temperature service.
High-temperature XRD can track the appearance and disappearance of phases during heating and thereby characterize transformation kinetics.
The exact Mg-depletion threshold for protective-film loss and the precipitation kinetics are unresolved.
Absence of a time- and temperature-dependent increase in intermetallic formation and Mg depletion correlated with performance loss would falsify the proposed mechanism.
